opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the key point is that the bottleneck people worry about, that we just don't have enough high-quality data for really hard, long-horizon tasks, is real, but it's less binding than it first appears, for a few reasons.

The first is that you don't necessarily need human demonstrations of the full complex task. A lot of what we've seen is that capability gets built up compositionally. If a model is very good at the pieces, like writing a function, reading a paper, checking a proof step, debugging an error, then chaining those together over longer horizons is partly a reliability problem rather than a whole new skill you need fresh data for. And reliability is something you can push on with scale, better scaffolding, and reinforcement learning.

The second is that for a lot of important domains you can generate your own training signal. Anywhere you have a checker, whether that's unit tests for code, a proof verifier for maths, or a simulator, you can have the model attempt things, see what works, and train on that. That loop doesn't depend on humans having written down how to do the task. It depends on being able to tell whether it was done well, and verification is often much easier than generation.

Third, and this is the one I find most important, AI research and engineering itself sits pretty squarely in that verifiable zone. Writing ML code, running experiments, reading off whether a loss went down: that's the kind of thing where you get a lot of feedback cheaply. So even if the systems are uneven, very strong on checkable technical work and weaker on fuzzy judgment, being strong in exactly that area could be enough to speed up the next round of progress considerably.

Now, I want to be honest about the uncertainty. There are tasks where the reward is genuinely hard to specify, long-term strategic judgment, things where outcomes take years to show up, and it's quite possible progress there stays slow. I wouldn't say I'm confident we get extremely capable systems in two to three years. But I don't think the data limitation rules it out, and given the stakes, I think we have to take that possibility seriously and plan for it rather than assume we have lots of slack.

That also connects to the safety work I care about. If capabilities run ahead in the domains where verification is easy, the open question becomes how we supervise these systems on the tasks where we can't easily check the answer ourselves. That's why I think scalable oversight approaches, things like debate, matter so much: they're aimed precisely at the gap between what models can do and what humans can directly verify.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the standard worry goes something like: we've essentially eaten the internet, and the internet is full of short, easy things — Reddit comments, Wikipedia articles, Stack Overflow answers. It is not full of worked examples of someone running a six-month research program, or managing a large engineering project, or doing the kind of long-horizon, messy, iterative work that we actually care about. So the argument is that you'll hit a wall: the models get very good at the stuff the data covers and then stall out on the hard, long tasks.

I think that argument has real force, but I'd push back on the conclusion for a few reasons.

The first is that the data limitation is a limitation on *demonstrations*, not on *feedback*. For a lot of the complex tasks we care about — coding, maths, a surprising amount of science — you don't need a human to show you the right answer, you need a way to check whether an answer is right. Does the code pass the tests, does the proof check, does the prediction match the experiment. Once you have that kind of signal, you can generate your own training data: the model tries things, some of them work, and you train on the ones that worked. That's roughly what's been happening with reasoning models, and it's why you see these very fast jumps on things like competition maths, where the pretraining data was never going to get you there by itself.

The second thing is that the gap between "lots of short examples" and "a few long ones" may be smaller than it looks. A long task is mostly made of short pieces glued together with some planning, error-correction, and memory. The short pieces are well covered. What's missing is the glue, and the glue turns out to be fairly generic — it's the same skill whether you're debugging a codebase or writing a paper. So you don't need millions of examples of each long task; you need enough signal that the model learns to not lose the thread, to notice when it's gone wrong, to go back. We've seen the length of task that models can handle roughly doubling every several months, and I don't see an obvious reason that stops.

The third is just that the labs are now very explicitly aware of this bottleneck and are spending enormous amounts of money on it. People are paying experts to produce long trajectories, they're building environments where agents can act and get feedback, they're using current models to generate and filter synthetic data for the next ones. Any time there's a known bottleneck and that much capital pointed at it, my prior is that it gets at least partially routed around.

Now, I want to be honest about the uncertainty here. Two to three years is my guess for "systems that can do a large fraction of what a good researcher or engineer does over weeks" — not a confident prediction. There are scenarios where the feedback signal is too noisy for genuinely open-ended work, where you can verify a proof but can't verify "was this a good research direction" without waiting years. Taste, judgement, knowing which problem to work on — those are the places I'd expect the data problem to bite hardest.

But I'd say the thing to notice is that the "we're out of data" argument has been made several times already, and each time the response has been a shift in *what kind* of data matters rather than a stall. And from a safety perspective, that's actually the point: I'd much rather plan for the world where this works and be wrong than plan for the wall and be surprised. The cost of being surprised in that direction is just a lot higher.

astra-6.text:
I think the key uncertainty is how much of the training data has to come from humans doing the task. If you need lots of examples of people successfully completing very difficult tasks, then clearly that’s a bottleneck. But there are other ways to get a training signal.

For example, in mathematics or programming, it can be much easier to check an answer than to produce it. A system can try lots of approaches, find out which ones work, and train on that experience. So a limited supply of human demonstrations doesn’t necessarily imply a limited supply of useful training data. The system can generate experience for itself.

The question is how far that generalises. There are plenty of important tasks where checking success is difficult, or where feedback takes a long time. So this isn’t an argument that extremely capable systems are definitely coming in two or three years. But I don’t think the shortage of human data for complex tasks is a strong enough reason to rule that out. If learning from automatically generated experience works well across enough domains, progress could be very fast.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between having examples of how to do a task and being able to tell whether the task was done well. We may not have much training data showing how to carry out a long, complicated research project. But if we can evaluate the result, we can potentially train systems by having them try things and learn from the feedback.

Coding is a useful example. You don’t necessarily need a human to write out every step of the solution if you can run the program and check whether it works. And as models get better, they can tackle harder problems and generate more useful training experience for themselves.

That doesn’t mean this will work equally well everywhere. In some areas, evaluating an answer is itself extremely difficult, and that could be a serious bottleneck. But I wouldn’t take the absence of human demonstrations for complex tasks as a strong reason to rule out very capable systems in two or three years. There are ways to learn beyond imitating the data we already have.
